# Hotjar vs OpenReplay (2026)

## Overview
Hotjar and OpenReplay are two popular tools used for session recording, heatmaps, and user feedback. These tools are beneficial for product managers, UX designers, and marketers who want to understand user behavior and improve their website's user experience. The core use case for both tools is to provide insights into user interactions, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Hotjar offers a free plan with limited features, while OpenReplay is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: OpenReplay allows users to retain full ownership of their data, while Hotjar stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Hotjar is generally easier to set up, while OpenReplay requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: OpenReplay is more scalable due to its self-hosted nature, while Hotjar can become expensive for large teams.
* Feature difference: OpenReplay offers more advanced filtering and segmentation options, while Hotjar has a more user-friendly interface.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Hotjar | OpenReplay |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $32-$80+/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $1,600-$4,000/year | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $6,400-$16,000/year | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Hotjar:**
* Easy to set up and use
* User-friendly interface
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Integrates with popular tools like Slack and Trello
* Limited control over data ownership
**OpenReplay:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Offers advanced filtering and segmentation options
* Scalable and customizable
* Retain full ownership of data
* Requires technical expertise to set up
* Limited integration with third-party tools

## When to Choose Each
Hotjar is suitable for small to medium-sized teams who want an easy-to-use tool with a user-friendly interface. It's ideal for teams who don't require advanced features and are willing to compromise on data ownership. On the other hand, OpenReplay is perfect for larger teams or organizations that require more control over their data and want a scalable solution. It's also suitable for teams with technical expertise who can handle the setup and customization process.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Hotjar in JSON format.
2. Set up an OpenReplay instance on your server.
3. Use the OpenReplay import tool to migrate your data from Hotjar.
4. Configure your OpenReplay instance to match your Hotjar setup.
5. Test your OpenReplay instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
OpenReplay is not yet production-ready for most users due to its technical requirements and limited documentation. However, for teams with technical expertise, OpenReplay offers a powerful and customizable solution. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that OpenReplay requires a significant amount of server resources to run smoothly. We recommend switching to OpenReplay if you're a technical team with specific requirements and don't mind the setup process.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams with technical expertise who want more control over their data
* Large teams who require a scalable solution and are willing to invest in setup and customization
* Organizations with strict data ownership requirements
* Teams who don't need advanced integration with third-party tools
* Developers who want a customizable and open-source solution

## FAQ
### What is the main difference between Hotjar and OpenReplay?
The main difference is that OpenReplay is free and self-hosted, while Hotjar offers a free plan with limited features and requires a subscription for full features.
### Is OpenReplay suitable for non-technical teams?
No, OpenReplay requires technical expertise to set up and customize.
### Can I integrate OpenReplay with third-party tools?
Yes, but the integration options are limited compared to Hotjar.
### How long does it take to migrate from Hotjar to OpenReplay?
The migration process can take several hours to several days, depending on the complexity of your setup.
### Is OpenReplay production-ready?
Not yet, due to its technical requirements and limited documentation.

# Loom vs Cap (2026)

## Overview
Loom and Cap are both video recording and sharing tools that help teams communicate more effectively. This comparison is beneficial for teams looking to switch from a proprietary, cloud-based solution to a self-hosted, open-source alternative. The core use case for both tools is to record and share videos, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Loom has a free plan and several paid plans, while Cap is free and open-source, with optional self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Loom stores data on its servers, while Cap allows users to host their own data.
* Setup complexity: Loom is easy to set up, while Cap requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Loom is designed for large teams, while Cap is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams.
* Integration: Loom integrates with more third-party apps, while Cap has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Loom | Cap |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $12.50-$14.99/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $12.50-$14.99/user/month (approximately $625-$749/month) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $12.50-$14.99/user/month (approximately $2,500-$2,998/month) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Loom:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Integrates with many third-party apps
* Scalable for large teams
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data
**Cap:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for data control
* Customizable
* Limited integrations
* Requires technical expertise to set up

## When to Choose Each
Loom is a good choice for large teams that need a scalable, easy-to-use video recording and sharing solution. It's also a good option for teams that don't mind storing their data on a proprietary server. Cap, on the other hand, is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that want more control over their data and are willing to invest time in setting up a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Loom videos in MP4 format.
2. Set up a Cap server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Cap import tool to upload your Loom videos to your Cap server.
4. Update any links or integrations to point to your new Cap server.
5. Test your Cap setup to ensure everything is working correctly.

## Our Take
Cap is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and manage. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Cap's video processing capabilities are not as robust as Loom's. However, for teams that value data control and customization, Cap is a good option. We recommend switching to Cap if you're a small to medium-sized team with technical expertise and a need for self-hosting.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced integrations
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that want more control over their data
* Teams with limited budgets that can't afford Loom's paid plans
* Teams with simple video recording needs that don't require advanced features
* Teams with in-house technical expertise that can handle self-hosting

## FAQ
### Can I use Cap for free?
Yes, Cap is free and open-source, with optional self-hosting.
### Is Cap as easy to use as Loom?
No, Cap requires more technical expertise to set up and manage.
### Can I integrate Cap with other tools?
Yes, but Cap's integrations are limited compared to Loom.
### How do I migrate my Loom videos to Cap?
You can export your Loom videos in MP4 format and use the Cap import tool to upload them to your Cap server.
### Is Cap suitable for large teams?
Not yet, as Cap is designed for small to medium-sized teams and may not be scalable enough for large teams.

# Canva vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Canva and Penpot are two popular graphic design and collaboration tools used by individuals, teams, and businesses to create visual content. This comparison is beneficial for users who want to switch from a proprietary platform to an open-source alternative, with a core use case of designing and collaborating on graphics, presentations, and web pages. The key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and design process.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Canva offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $15/user/month, while Penpot is free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data, whereas Canva stores user data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Canva has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Penpot is more scalable due to its open-source nature and self-hosting capabilities.
* Feature difference: Canva has a more extensive template library, while Penpot has a more flexible and customizable design engine.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Canva | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $15-$30/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $15-$30/user/month * 50 = $750-$1500/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $15-$30/user/month * 200 = $3000-$6000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Canva:**
* Easy to use and intuitive interface
* Large template library and design assets
* Collaborative features and real-time commenting
* Integrations with popular platforms and tools
* Limited control over data and design process
**Penpot:**
* Open-source and self-hosting capabilities
* Customizable and flexible design engine
* Free and cost-effective
* Community-driven development and support
* Steeper learning curve and limited template library

## When to Choose Each
Canva is suitable for small to medium-sized teams and individuals who prioritize ease of use, a large template library, and collaborative features. It's ideal for those who don't require full control over their data and design process. On the other hand, Penpot is suitable for larger teams, enterprises, and organizations that require scalability, customization, and data ownership. It's ideal for those who value open-source software, self-hosting, and community-driven development.

## Migration Path
1. Export your designs from Canva in PNG or PDF format.
2. Set up a Penpot instance on your server or use a cloud provider.
3. Import your designs into Penpot using the built-in import tool.
4. Update your design assets and templates to take advantage of Penpot's customizable design engine.
5. Train your team on using Penpot and its features.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some features and polish compared to Canva. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's collaborative features are still in development, and real-time commenting is not yet available. However, for teams and organizations that value open-source software, self-hosting, and data ownership, Penpot is a clear choice. We recommend switching to Penpot if you're a larger team or enterprise with specific design and collaboration requirements.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of 10-20 users who don't need advanced collaborative features
* Medium-sized teams of 50-100 users who require customization and scalability
* Enterprises with 200+ users who need self-hosting and data ownership
* Design agencies who value open-source software and community-driven development
* Educational institutions who require free and cost-effective design tools

## FAQ
### Is Penpot free?
Yes, Penpot is free and open-source. It's available for self-hosting, and there are no per-user costs.
### Can I import my Canva designs into Penpot?
Yes, you can import your Canva designs into Penpot using the built-in import tool. However, some features and formatting may not be preserved.
### Is Penpot suitable for small teams?
Yes, Penpot is suitable for small teams, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and use.
### Does Penpot have a large template library?
No, Penpot's template library is still in development and not as extensive as Canva's.
### Is Penpot available for self-hosting?
Yes, Penpot is available for self-hosting, and you can set it up on your server or use a cloud provider.

# Canva vs Inkscape

## Overview

Popular web-based design platform for creating graphics, presentations, and marketing materials. is a popular proprietary tool in the design space. Inkscape is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Canva costs Free / $15-$30/user/month; Inkscape is Free
- **License**: Canva is Proprietary; Inkscape is GPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: Inkscape can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Inkscape eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Inkscape has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Canva | Inkscape |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $15-$30/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Canva

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Inkscape

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [inkscape/inkscape](https://github.com/inkscape/inkscape) * ~4k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Canva if:** Canva is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Inkscape if:** Inkscape is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Canva in its standard export format, review Inkscape import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Inkscape is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Canva tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Inkscape instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Canva, switching to self-hosted Inkscape will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Canva until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Canva paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Inkscape free to use?
Yes. Inkscape is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Canva to Inkscape?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Canva data, follow the Inkscape import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Inkscape get regular updates?
Yes. Inkscape has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Inkscape without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Inkscape development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Canva](https://canva.com) and [Inkscape](https://inkscape.org) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Inkscape is a free, self-hosted alternative to Canva. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

## Overview
Sketch and Penpot are two popular design tools used for user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) design. The core use case for both tools is to create and collaborate on digital product designs.

* Cost: Sketch has a monthly subscription fee, while Penpot is free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data, while Sketch stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, while Sketch is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Sketch is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Penpot is more suitable for smaller teams and individuals.
* Feature difference: Penpot has a built-in commenting and collaboration feature, while Sketch requires a separate plugin for this functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Sketch | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $450-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1800-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Sketch:**
* Easy to use and intuitive interface
* Large community of users and plugins available
* Robust features for design and collaboration
* Integrates well with other design tools
* Limited control over data and self-hosting
**Penpot:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting available for full data control
* Built-in commenting and collaboration features
* Customizable and extensible
* Limited support and resources compared to Sketch

## When to Choose Each
Sketch is suitable for large teams and enterprises that require a robust and scalable design solution, with a focus on ease of use and integration with other design tools. Penpot, on the other hand, is ideal for smaller teams, individuals, and organizations that value data control and customization, and are willing to invest time in setting up and maintaining their own instance.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Sketch designs in SVG or JSON format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your designs to Penpot.
3. Configure your Penpot instance to match your Sketch workflow, including setting up users and permissions.
4. Update any plugins or integrations to work with Penpot.
5. Test and refine your Penpot setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some features and polish compared to Sketch. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's performance can degrade with very large designs or complex projects. However, for teams that value data control and customization, and are willing to invest time in setting up and maintaining their own instance, Penpot is a viable alternative to Sketch.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced collaboration features
* Individuals who want full control over their design data
* Organizations with strict data security requirements
* Teams that require customization and extensibility
* Users who are already familiar with open-source design tools

## FAQ
### Can I use Penpot for free?
Yes, Penpot is free and open-source, with no subscription fees.
### Is Penpot compatible with Sketch files?
Yes, Penpot can import Sketch files in SVG or JSON format.
### Can I self-host Penpot?
Yes, Penpot can be self-hosted on your own servers.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams?
Not yet, as Penpot is still developing its scalability and performance features.
### Can I use Penpot for other design tasks besides UI/UX?
Yes, Penpot can be used for other design tasks, such as graphic design and illustration.

# Adobe Premiere Pro vs Kdenlive (2026)

## Overview
Adobe Premiere Pro and Kdenlive are two video editing tools used for creating professional-looking videos. The core use case for both tools is video editing, with Adobe Premiere Pro being a industry-standard and Kdenlive being a popular open-source option.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Adobe Premiere Pro requires a monthly subscription, while Kdenlive is free.
* Data Ownership: Adobe Premiere Pro stores project files in a proprietary format, while Kdenlive uses an open standard.
* Setup Complexity: Adobe Premiere Pro has a more straightforward setup process, while Kdenlive requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: Adobe Premiere Pro is designed for large-scale video production, while Kdenlive is better suited for smaller projects.
* Multi-camera Editing: Adobe Premiere Pro has a more advanced multi-camera editing feature, while Kdenlive's implementation is more basic.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Adobe Premiere Pro | Kdenlive |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $20.99-$54.99/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $1049.50-$2749.50/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4199.80-$10999.80/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Adobe Premiere Pro:**
* Industry-standard video editing tool
* Advanced features like multi-camera editing and color grading
* Seamless integration with other Adobe tools
* Large community of users and resources
* Regular updates with new features
**Kdenlive:**
* Free and open-source
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Supports a wide range of video and audio formats
* Cross-platform compatibility
* Limited resources and community compared to Adobe Premiere Pro

## When to Choose Each
Adobe Premiere Pro is the better choice for large video production teams or individuals who require advanced features like multi-camera editing and color grading. It is also a good option for those already invested in the Adobe ecosystem. Kdenlive, on the other hand, is a great option for small teams or individuals on a budget, or those who value the freedom and customizability of an open-source tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Adobe Premiere Pro project as an EDL (Edit Decision List) file.
2. Import the EDL file into Kdenlive using the "Import" menu.
3. Re-link your media files to the corresponding files on your system.
4. Adjust your project settings and editing timeline to match your original project.
5. Export your final video in the desired format.

## Our Take
Kdenlive is a production-ready tool for most users, but it may lack some of the polish and refinement of Adobe Premiere Pro. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Kdenlive's color grading tools are not as advanced as those in Adobe Premiere Pro. However, for many users, Kdenlive's free and open-source nature, combined with its high customizability and extensibility, make it a compelling alternative to Adobe Premiere Pro.

## Who Should Switch
* Small video production teams (less than 10 people) who do not need advanced features like multi-camera editing
* Individuals on a budget who want a free video editing tool
* Teams who value the freedom and customizability of an open-source tool
* Those who do not need seamless integration with other Adobe tools
* Educational institutions or non-profits who want a cost-effective video editing solution

Yes, Kdenlive can be used for commercial video production, and its free and open-source nature makes it a cost-effective option.

Yes, Kdenlive is available for Windows, as well as Linux and macOS.

Yes, Kdenlive can import Adobe Premiere Pro projects via the EDL file format.

Yes, Kdenlive supports 4K video editing, as well as other high-resolution formats.

# Figma vs Inkscape (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Inkscape are two popular design tools used for creating and editing vector graphics. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from a cloud-based, proprietary tool like Figma to a free, open-source alternative like Inkscape. The core use case for both tools is graphic design, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Inkscape is completely free.
* Data Ownership: Figma stores designs on its servers, while Inkscape allows users to store designs locally or on their own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a simpler setup process, while Inkscape requires more technical expertise to install and configure.
* Scalability: Figma is more scalable, with better support for large teams and complex designs, while Inkscape can become slower with very large files.
* Feature Difference: Figma has a more comprehensive set of collaboration features, including real-time commenting and @mentions, while Inkscape has more advanced vector editing capabilities.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Inkscape |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ Easy to use and set up
	+ Collaborative features like real-time commenting and @mentions
	+ Scalable and performant
	+ Integrates well with other design tools
	+ Large community of users and developers
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over data storage and ownership
	+ Limited advanced vector editing capabilities
	+ Proprietary license
	+ Limited self-hosting options
### Inkscape
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Advanced vector editing capabilities
	+ Customizable and extensible
	+ Self-hosting options available
	+ Cross-platform compatibility
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited collaboration features
	+ Can be slower with very large files
	+ Limited integration with other design tools
	+ Smaller community of users and developers

## When to Choose Each
Figma is a good choice for large teams or enterprises that require a scalable, collaborative design tool with advanced features like real-time commenting and @mentions. It's also a good choice for designers who are already familiar with the tool and have invested in its ecosystem. Inkscape, on the other hand, is a good choice for individuals or small teams who want a free, open-source design tool with advanced vector editing capabilities. It's also a good choice for designers who value control over their data and want to self-host their designs.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs as SVG files.
2. Install Inkscape on your local machine or server.
3. Import the SVG files into Inkscape using the "File" > "Import" menu.
4. Update any broken links or references to external files.
5. Take advantage of Inkscape's advanced vector editing capabilities to refine your designs.

## Our Take
Inkscape is not yet production-ready for most users, due to its limited collaboration features and steeper learning curve. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Inkscape can be slower with very large files, which can make it less suitable for complex designs. However, for designers who value control over their data and want a free, open-source design tool with advanced vector editing capabilities, Inkscape is a good choice.

Inkscape has made significant progress in recent years, but it still lags behind Figma in terms of scalability and collaboration features. Designers who require these features may want to stick with Figma or explore other alternatives. On the other hand, designers who prioritize data ownership and advanced vector editing capabilities may find Inkscape to be a good fit.

For designers who are considering switching from Figma to Inkscape, we recommend carefully evaluating their needs and requirements before making the switch. If you're a small team or individual designer who values control over your data and wants a free, open-source design tool, Inkscape may be a good choice. However, if you're a large team or enterprise that requires a scalable, collaborative design tool with advanced features, Figma may still be the better option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams or individuals who want a free, open-source design tool with advanced vector editing capabilities
* Designers who value control over their data and want to self-host their designs
* Teams who don't require advanced collaboration features like real-time commenting and @mentions
* Designers who are already familiar with Inkscape or have experience with other open-source design tools
* Teams who are looking to reduce costs and don't mind a steeper learning curve

## FAQ
### Can I use Inkscape for collaborative design projects?
No, Inkscape is not well-suited for collaborative design projects, as it lacks advanced collaboration features like real-time commenting and @mentions.

### Is Inkscape compatible with Figma files?
Yes, Inkscape can import SVG files exported from Figma, but may not support all Figma features or formatting.

### Can I self-host Inkscape on my own server?
Yes, Inkscape can be self-hosted on your own server, giving you full control over your data and designs.

### Is Inkscape free to use?
Yes, Inkscape is completely free to use, with no costs or licensing fees.

### Can I use Inkscape on multiple platforms?
Yes, Inkscape is cross-platform compatible, and can be used on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
